blocks.text: Then the firmness of the valves gives way, loosened by the inner heat. And soon, vomiting up what had previously been bound shut, they tear apart the flesh, no longer protected by its shelly shield, in an unequal fight. It must be admitted, however, that Plutarch, in the book Utra anim., attributes this same thing to herons, when he says that the art of opening oysters is owed τοῖς ἐρωδίων σοφίσμασιν· ὅταν γὰρ τὴν κόγχην καταπίῃ μεμυκυῖαν, ἐνοχλούμενος ἐγκαρτερεῖ, μέχρις ἂν αἴσθηται μαλασσομένην, καὶ χαλῶσαν ὑπὸ τῆς θερμότητος· τότε δὲ ἐκβαλὼν κεχηνυῖαν, καὶ ἀπεσπασμένην, ἐξεῖλε τὸ ἐδώδιμον [tois erōdiōn sophismasin; hotan gar tēn konchēn katapiē memykuian, enochloumenos enkarterei, mechris an aisthētai malassomenēn, kai chalōsan hypo tēs thermotētos; tote de ekbalōn kechēnuian, kai apespasmenēn, exeile to edōdimon], to the ingenuity of herons: for when the heron has swallowed a closed shell, although it finds it troublesome, it nevertheless endures it until it feels it softened and loosened by the heat; then, casting it out gaping and torn open, it takes the edible part out of it. And Aelian, book 3, chapter 24, after relating that storks offer their own food, vomited up, to their young if nothing else is available with which to feed them, adds καὶ τοὺς ἐρωδίους ποιεῖν [III, 45] ταὐτὸ, καὶ τοὺς πελεκᾶνας μέντοι [kai tous erōdious poiein tauto, kai tous pelekanas mentoi], that herons too, and pelicans, do the same. But what we have said about pelicans is celebrated by constant report and by everyone's talk, whereas what Plutarch and Aelian write about herons and storks is very obscure, and has no other authorities, as far as I remember. Indeed, I would think that by the name herons Plutarch means pelicans, which many count among the herons, because the pelican differs from the heron almost only in its bill, which it has broader at the tip and in the shape of a spoon ^{(5)}. Gesner: It certainly seems to me that our pelican should be counted in the heron kind, from which it differs not so much by any other mark as by the breadth of its bill. Likewise: Albertus also thought that the bird which we call the spoonbill (that is, the pelican) was the white heron. Turner: If I had not seen the albardeola (that is, the white heron) in Italy, I would have judged the English shovelard (that is, the pelican) to be the albardeola. For Belon too, book 4 De Avibus, chapter 5, Aristotle's λευκερώδιος [leukerōdios] (that is, white heron) is the bird which from the shape of its bill they call pale poche ou cullier, that is, the pelican of the ancients. Plutarch, therefore, could on the same grounds take herons and pelicans indiscriminately. Or, if it is true that the heron too, like the pelican, vomits up shells ^{(6)}, as Plutarch holds, why could the Hebrew name קאת kaath, formed from vomiting, not have been common to the heron and the pelican, since they are kindred birds and alike in so many respects?

Granting this, these words of the Psalmist, Psalm. CII, 7, will be plainer: Because of the voice of my groaning my bones have cleaved to my flesh; I have become like the kaath of the wilderness; I have been like the chos of the desolate places. In these he compares himself, on account of his laments and groans, to two birds, namely the kaath and the chos. From this one may infer that these birds have something plaintive and groaning about them. And among the many reasons which almost persuade us that the chos is the onocrotalus, this was one: that the onocrotalus is a bird of dreadful voice, which admirably imitates the wailing of a man in grievous pain. [III, 46] Accordingly, so that the Psalmist be consistent, the same must be shown of the bird kaath too. This will be difficult if kaath means nothing but the pelican, since nothing whatever is found about the voice of the pelican. But if the name kaath is common to the heron and the pelican, [col. 296] which I think agrees with the truth, it will be easy to find a way out. For the heron has a loud voice ^{(7)}. Homer calls it a clangor, and in Iliad 10 he says of the heron which Pallas sent as a favourable omen to Diomedes and Ulysses as they went by night to the enemy camp:
— — — τοὶ δ' οὐ ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσι Νύκτα δι' ὀρφναίην, ἀλλὰ κλάγξαντος ἄκουσαν· [— — — toi d' ou idon ophthalmoisi / Nykta di' orphnaiēn, alla klanxantos akousan;]

They did not see it with their eyes through the dark night, but heard it clanging. And the Philosopher, on the ash-coloured heron, History book 9, chapter 1: Τούτων (ἐρωδίων) ὁ πέλλος χαλεπῶς εὐνάζει τε, καὶ ὀχεύει. κράζει τε γὰρ, καὶ αἷμα, ὥς φασιν, ἀφίησιν ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ὀχεύων, καὶ τίκτει φαυλῶς, ὡς καὶ ὀδυνηρῶς. [Toutōn (erōdiōn) ho pellos chalepōs eunazei te, kai ocheuei. krazei te gar, kai haima, hōs phasin, aphiēsin ek tōn ophthalmōn ocheuōn, kai tiktei phaulōs, hōs kai odynērōs.] Which Pliny, book 1, chapter 60, renders thus: These suffer anguish in coupling. The males indeed shed blood from their eyes with loud cries; nor do the females give birth with less difficulty. But, what is most to be noted, the starry heron, or stellaris, which is commonly called the butaurus [bittern], is a bird whose bellowing is so dreadful that in this respect it scarcely yields to the onocrotalus. It is strange that the ancients were silent about this, unless these words of Pliny, book 10, chapter 42, refer to it: There is one that imitates the lowing of oxen in the territory of Arles, called the bull. And those of the author of the Philomela:
And in the marshy waters the butio booms.
